newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge condemn and "sentence" Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge condemn and "sentence" Pol Pot.

text.p: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said in a radio broadcast on Saturday that former leader Pol Pot had been condemned and sentenced for unspecified crimes.
The radio, monitored in Phnom Penh, said Pol Pot had been condemned for serious deeds against the people and the nation, but did not say what his sentence was.
"Thousands of people held a meeting to condemn and sentence Pol Pot...(for his) serious and rebellious deeds against the people and the nation," the radio said.
The radio did not say if Pol Pot was present at the meeting, but broadcast sounds of the crowd denouncing him.
Pol Pot was the mastermind of the 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror during which more than a million Cambodians were executed or died of starvation, disease, or hard labour.
The Khmer Rouge underwent a violent split in June and days later Pol Pot was denounced over Khmer Rouge radio and later hunted down and captured by his former comrades.
Khmer Rouge political leader Khieu Samphan announced over the radio on July 5 that Pol Pot was politically finished and that the guerrillas recognised the Cambodian constitution.
A commander at the rebels' Anlong Veng base in northern Cambodia said in the Saturday broadcast that the Khmer Rouge could no longer be called the "Pol Pot regime".
"Now our movement is no longer the so-called Pol Pot regime," the commander, identified as Kham Ngon, said in the broadcast.
"We will not follow this regime any more and we have to destroy this regime in order to liberate our people," the commander said.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh was negotiating with the Khmer Rouge faction that broke with Pol Pot to secure the guerrilla leader's handover.
But the bloody takeover and ouster of Ranariddh on July 6 by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen brought those talks to an abrupt end.
Ranariddh said earlier he was willing to form an alliance with Khieu Samphan, infuriating Hun Sen, who analysts said wanted to prevent any deal that would bolster his rival's position.

Hun Sen declared the prince's negotiations with the Khmer Rouge illegal and justified his move against Ranariddh's forces on July 5 by saying Ranariddh's military commanders were bringing defectors from the guerrilla group into the capital.
Hun Sen and Ranariddh agreed in late June that if Pol Pot was ever handed over to the government he should be brought before an international court.
The new Cambodian government still wants to try to bring Pol Pot to justice before an international court, a senior government official said on Wednesday.
The guerrillas' clandestine radio, its main propaganda mouthpiece, has broadcast attacks on Hun Sen since his ouster of Ranariddh, condemning him as a puppet of Vietnam.
The Khmer Rouge boycotted a 1993 election because they said the former Hanoi-backed government, led by Hun Sen, was not dismantled as stipulated in a Paris peace agreement.
In recent years, many rebels defected to the government.
